headline_seed: California Voters Reject Prop. 40 Billionaire Tax Measure - The New York Times

consensus_facts: California voters rejected Proposition 40, a measure to tax the wealth of billionaires (confirmed by BBC, CBS News, and The Guardian body text).
Prop. 40 would have levied a one-time 5% tax on California residents with a net worth of more than $1 billion (confirmed by BBC, CBS News, and The Guardian).

Supporters framed the tax as a way to offset federal healthcare cuts stemming from President Trump's tax-and-spending law (the 'One Big Beautiful Bill Act' per CBS News and The Guardian; BBC references Trump's tax and spending bill).
Proponents projected the tax would raise roughly $100 billion (BBC says ~$100bn; CBS News says ~$100 billion over five years).
The measure was principally sponsored by the healthcare union SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West (confirmed by CBS News and The Guardian).
Governor Gavin Newsom opposed the measure, citing concerns that it would drive the wealthy out of the state and reduce income tax revenue (confirmed by BBC, CBS News, and The Guardian).

Google co-founder Sergey Brin was a leading donor to the opposition campaign, contributing more than $100 million (BBC cites more than $100m; The Guardian cites at least $132m; CBS News names Brin among opponents).

The opposition campaign was the most expensive of its kind in California history, with figures cited in the hundreds of millions of dollars (The Guardian cites ~$425m; CBS News cites over $250 million for Building a Better California as of Oct. 28).

Two companion measures, Propositions 41 and 42, were designed so that if either received more 'Yes' votes than Prop. 40, they would block the billionaire tax from taking effect even if it passed (confirmed by CBS News and The Guardian).
Proposition 41 was also rejected by voters (confirmed by CBS News).
The measure divided Democrats and traditional allies, including labor unions (confirmed by BBC, CBS News, and The Guardian).

positions.The Guardian: Billionaires mounted a nearly $425m battle against Prop 40, the most expensive opposition campaign in state history.
positions.CBS News: Building a Better California raised over $250 million against the billionaire tax as of Oct. 28.
positions.Associated Press (headline-only, via Cal: Billionaires spent $378 million to kill California's wealth tax.

positions.BBC News: Brin gave more than $100m to a political organisation funding ballot measures that could block the tax.
positions.The Guardian: Brin contributed at least $132m to fight the tax, per campaign finance filings.

positions.CBS News: Proponents projected $100 billion over five years, but a Stanford study concluded it may generate only about $30 billion.
positions.The Guardian: Does not provide a revenue projection figure.

disagreements.topic: Scope of what the tax applied to

positions.BBC News: A 5% tax on total wealth, including assets such as shares as well as income.
positions.CBS News: A 5% tax on net worth of $1 billion, excluding real estate and certain retirement assets.
positions.The Guardian: A 5% tax on all individuals with a net worth of more than $1bn as of 1 January 2026.

positions.CBS News: Opposed by Newsom, former Rep. Katie Porter, the California Medical Association, and the California Teachers Association.
positions.The Guardian: Opposed by both the Democratic and Republican candidates for governor and Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California; backed by Bernie Sanders and Ro Khanna.

framing_analysis.Associated Press: This entry is a Google News RSS aggregation listing multiple outlet headlines rather than an AP article body. It provides no retrievable AP body text — only a cluster of headlines (AP, CalMatters, Washington Post, NYT, NBC News, Fox Business, LA Times, Yahoo, Mercury News). Headline framings range from neutral ('California voters reject measure to tax the wealth of billionaires') to money-focused (CalMatters: 'Billionaires spent $378 million to kill California's wealth tax. It worked') to politically-framed (NBC: 'in a blow to the left') to economic-threat framing (Fox Business: 'one-two punch as voters reject wealth tax and billionaires eye exits'). Treat only as a headline index, not a body source.
framing_analysis.NPR: Headline-only. Frames the story around intra-Democratic division ('billionaire tax proposal that divided Democrats'), emphasizing the political split rather than the outcome's magnitude. No body text available.
framing_analysis.BBC News: Leads on the rejection and the 'world's first' billionaire wealth tax angle, giving international context (California's economy ranks fourth globally, high concentration of billionaires and high wealth gap). Names celebrity billionaires (Zuckerberg, Kardashian, Winfrey) for color. Emphasizes Newsom's and labor unions' opposition and that some billionaires physically moved out of state. Quotes union leader Dave Regan pledging a 2028 revival. Balanced but gives notable weight to the billionaires-fled-the-state narrative.
framing_analysis.CBS News (Prop. 40 article): The most detailed and balanced body text in the dossier. Leads on the projection of defeat and the record-shattering spending and allied split. Carefully presents both sides: cites the Stanford study undercutting the $100B estimate (projecting ~$30B) AND counters with Nobel economists (Acemoglu, Stiglitz) supporting the measure. Names opposition donors extensively (Brin, Page, Doerr, Thiel, Khosla, Collison) and includes a supportive billionaire quote from Nvidia's Jensen Huang. Explains the Prop 41/42 mechanics in detail.
framing_analysis.CBS News (Prop. 41 article): Procedural companion piece. Focuses narrowly on the mechanics of Prop. 41 — state auditor reviews, spending-limit changes, four-year audits — and confirms both Prop. 40 and Prop. 41 were rejected. Frames Prop. 41 as a potential invalidating mechanism for the billionaire tax.
framing_analysis.CBS News (Prop. 45 article): A separate ballot-measure story about CEQA environmental review reform, tangential to the billionaire tax. Included likely due to the shared election. Balanced coverage quoting both the Center for Biological Diversity (opposition) and the California Chamber of Commerce (support), and noting the pro-housing community's split. Does not bear directly on Prop. 40.
framing_analysis.The Guardian: Leads on the framing of billionaires winning and the 'most expensive campaign in state history' angle, foregrounding Silicon Valley money ('flush with Silicon Valley dollars'). Emphasizes the opposition's 'everyone tax' messaging and the national stakes ('could hamper nationwide momentum on demands that billionaires pay their fair share'). Notably includes progressive backers (Bernie Sanders, Ro Khanna) and the 'poison pill' characterization of Props 41/42 by supporters. Most explicitly frames the result through an inequality/billionaire-influence lens.

primary_source_alignment: No primary sources (official election results, campaign finance filings, the Stanford study, or the economists' open letter) were located for this story. All figures — spending totals, Brin's contribution, the $100B vs. $30B revenue estimates — are reported secondhand by outlets and could not be verified against underlying documents.

Alignment between reports and the underlying ballot/vote certification cannot be assessed; outlets are citing projections (CBS News and AP 'project' the result) rather than final certified counts, and BBC notes it took nearly a week of counting.
missing_context: No outlet in the dossier reports the actual vote margin or percentage by which Prop. 40 was rejected — the results are described only as projections.

The status of Proposition 42 (the companion measure that would have banned any taxation on billionaire wealth) is not confirmed as passed or rejected in any body text; only Prop. 41's rejection is confirmed by CBS News.

Spending figures vary widely across sources (~$250M, $378M, ~$425M) with no single reconciled total or shared campaign-finance source cited, making the 'most expensive campaign in history' claim hard to pin to one number.
The Stanford study's methodology and the economists' open letter are each cited by only one outlet (CBS News), and no outlet links to or quotes the primary documents directly.
Article 1 (labeled 'Associated Press') is actually a Google News RSS headline aggregation, not an AP article — no genuine AP body text was retrievable, which limits wire-level corroboration.

No outlet details the precise exclusions (real estate, retirement assets) consistently — BBC and CBS News describe the tax base differently, and no source reconciles which assets were actually covered.
No article explains what happens next for the SEIU-promised 2028 effort beyond the pledge itself (reported only by BBC).
brief.suggested_post_type_reason: Three outlets (BBC, CBS News, The Guardian) reported the same result with materially different framings — ranging from an international 'world's first tax' angle to an inequality/billionaire-influence lens to an economic-flight narrative — and key figures like total spending and Brin's contribution diverge across sources with no primary document to reconcile them, making this a coverage-report story rather than a straight REPORT.
